table.name: individual_level
table.grain: One row per country x year x indicator x unit x individual-type breakdown. Breakdowns overlap; filter, never sum.

unit.label: Unit, i.e. the base population the percentage is a share of
unit.note: The other half of the metric's identity. Every unit here is a percentage; what differs is the population it is a percentage of - see codes[...].base, and codes[...].weightable for whether enterprise_count is its denominator.

PC_IND_IU3.label: Percentage of individuals who used internet in the last 3 months

PC_IND_IUAI.label: Percentage of individuals who have used any generative AI tools in the last 3 months

value.label: Observed value
value.note: Always a percentage (0-100), but of a base population that varies by unit. Read unit.codes[...].base before comparing two values, and see the mixed_denominators caveat: identical-looking numbers can have different meanings.

ind_type.label: Individual type (raw Eurostat breakdown code)
ind_type.note: Eurostat packs sex, age, education, labour status and citizenship into this one dimension. The sex/age/education columns decode the demographic subset; codes expressing something else decode to null.

caveats: Rows are overlapping subsets, not a partition: the same person is counted under IND_TOTAL, an age band, a sex band and an education band. Filter these rows, never sum them.

Every value is a percentage, but of 18 different base populations (see each unit's `base`). PC_ENT is a share of all enterprises; PC_ENT_AI_EC is a share only of those that considered AI. Both render as 0-100 and look comparable. Only compare or chart values that share the same base.
There is no population-count column. Unlike the firm-level table, these percentages cannot be converted into absolute numbers of people - no equivalent of the sbs_sc_ovw universe is wired up.
The unit of observation is a person, not a business. Never join or concatenate these rows with firm_level: comparing them is the point, merging them is a category error.
